title: Cubism, Surrealism and Abstract Art
summary: Cubism began in Paris about 1907 and was the most important trend at the start of the 20th century; Cezanne was its pioneer ('everything in nature must be treated as a cylinder or sphere'); its important artists were Picasso, Braque and Leger. They chose still life, landscapes and portraits and broke the motifs into small parts; the aim was construction and form in geometrical shapes, not emotion or richness of colour; forms became more abstract and general; the movement ended about 1920. Surrealism started in 1924 and continued till 1955; surrealist artists used images of the unconscious in their works; they were influenced by psycho-analysis and the movement grew out of the Dadaists' revolt; the most famous were Giorgio de Chirico and Salvador Dali. Abstract art is non-representational art that rejects realistic depiction of the world; it began about 1910 in the West; its pioneers are Kandinsky, Delaunay and Mondrian. Though these movements began in the West, they left a deep impression on Indian artists.

Artist: Pablo Picasso (born 1881 in Malaga, Spain; painter, sculptor and ceramist). Medium: oil on canvas. Date: 1912. Size: 100 x 73 cm. Collection: Philadelphia Museum of Art. Picasso followed the principles of abstract composition and was influenced by symbolism. His Blue Period (1900–02) is named after the blue-green tone of his canvases; his Rose Period (1905–07) used mainly pink; later his works were influenced by African artefacts, and from 1915 he developed his Cubist phase, which made him world famous. Cubism breaks three-dimensional forms into flat areas of pattern and colour so that shapes and parts of the body are seen from front and back together. 'Man with Violin' is a fine example of Analytical Cubism: the object is divided into parts showing different viewpoints at the same time, forms are recognisable but broken into cube-like forms; the human figure holding the violin is broken into geometrical shapes and rearranged; the colours are shades of brown and green; there is a continuous unity of form and colour. His best-known work is 'Guernica' on the Spanish Civil War.

Artist: Salvador Dali, the most famous Surrealist (Spanish painter, film maker and writer, died 1989). Medium: oil on canvas. Date: 1931. Size: 9½ x 13 inches. Collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York. Dali used a highly realistic, academic and precise technique, but his subject matter came from dreams and nightmares and showed the absurd, unusual and strange. The bare landscape and calm may be life after all wars; the only objects that suggest life are the 'melting clocks', which look realistic and create the sense of a disturbed mind; ants crawl over a watch as over rotting food. No Dali painting represents reality; objects look out of place. Other Surrealist works: 'Small Bottle of Rum' and 'Honey is Sweeter than Blood'.

Artist: Wassily Kandinsky (born 1866 in Russia, died 1944 in Paris), painter and art theoretician, a founder of abstract painting. Medium: oil on canvas. Date: December 1913. Size: 4 ft 3 in x 4 ft 3½ in. Collection: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York. He laid the foundation of non-representational art with three series – Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions – and wanted painting to be abstract like music. Other works: 'Accompanied Contrast', 'Yellow Accompaniment', 'Angular Structure'. In 'Black Lines' black paint (not Indian ink) is used; a group of lines in one corner takes different meaning according to arrangement; the coloured spots look as if applied by the fingers of a giant hand. Line, shape and colour have their own meaning; lines are sketchy and seem to have lives of their own.

vsa: Mention two of Picasso's famous periods.
The Blue Period (1900–02), named after the blue-green tone of his canvases, and the Rose Period (1905–07), in which he used mainly pink; also his Cubist phase, from which he became world famous.

Write a short note on Abstract Art.

Abstract art is a general term for non-representational art that rejects realistic depiction of the world. It began about 1910 and its pioneers are Kandinsky, Delaunay and Mondrian, who gave pictured form to abstract ideas that cannot be shown realistically.
October 2022
Describe the painting 'Persistence of Memory'.

Salvador Dali painted it in 1931 (oil on canvas, Museum of Modern Art, New York). A bare, calm landscape holds melting clocks with ants crawling over a watch, expressing a disturbed mind and the world of dreams; the technique is realistic but the objects are out of place.
sa: Give a note on the painting 'Black Lines' by Kandinsky.

'Black Lines' (oil on canvas, December 1913, Guggenheim Museum, New York) is an abstract composition in which black paint lines in one corner take different meanings according to their arrangement, with coloured spots that look applied by the fingers of a giant hand. It shows simplicity and pure diagrams, like skeletons without flesh; line, shape and colour have their own meaning and the lines seem to have lives of their own.
Briefly describe Salvador Dali's contribution to Surrealism.

Dali was the most famous Surrealist painter, a Spanish painter, film maker and writer. He used a highly realistic, academic and precise technique to depict the world of absurd, strange and dream-like elements and an unconventional grouping of objects with symbolic meaning. 'Persistence of Memory', 'Small Bottle of Rum' and 'Honey is Sweeter than Blood' are his works.
Write in brief about Pablo Picasso.

Picasso (born 1881 in Malaga, Spain) was a painter, sculptor and ceramist who followed abstract composition. His Blue Period (1900–02) and Rose Period (1905–07) were followed by African influence and the Cubist phase, which made him world famous; 'Man with Violin' (1912) is analytical cubism; 'Guernica' shows the Spanish Civil War.
la: What is Surrealism? Choose any one painting of Pablo Picasso and describe it.

Surrealism (1924–55) was a movement in which artists used images of the unconscious, influenced by psycho-analysis and arising from the Dadaists' revolt; Dali and de Chirico were the leading painters. Picasso's 'Man with Violin' (1912, oil on canvas, 100 x 73 cm, Philadelphia Museum of Art) is a fine example of Analytical Cubism: the man holding the violin is broken into geometrical shapes showing different viewpoints at once, in shades of brown and green, with unity of form and colour.
What is analytical cubism? Describe a famous painting of this style.

Analytical Cubism divides an object into parts showing different viewpoints at the same time; forms are recognisable but broken into cube-like forms. 'Man with Violin' (Picasso, 1912) breaks the human form with the violin into geometrical shapes arranged together, painted in browns and greens with a continuous unity of form and colour.
Define Cubism in art. Choose any painting of Kandinsky and describe it.

Cubism, begun in Paris about 1907 with Cezanne as pioneer and Picasso, Braque and Leger as artists, breaks forms into geometrical shapes and stresses construction, not emotion. Kandinsky's 'Black Lines' (1913, oil on canvas) is an abstract work of black lines and coloured spots in which line, shape and colour have their own meaning.
